#8771. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

#8770. Runners of All Fitness Levels Benefit From the Run/Walk Method. Here’s How to Use It to Pace Smarter and Race Faster.

Think you’re too advanced for the run/walk method? Think again.

Many experienced runners often assume that the run/walk method is only suitable for beginners. There’s no way it could help you reach your goals or allow you to run faster paces, right? In reality, it could be the missing piece of your training and racing plan.

Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Charlotte, North Carolina, believes run/walk has a place in your training—no matter your fitness level or your goals. In fact, she includes some form of the run/walk method in all her runners’ training, because it’s a tried-and-true strategy for tackling longer distances, recovering more efficiently, and even dropping minutes from your marathon time.

So whether you’re a couch-to-5K runner, a first-time marathoner, or a seasoned athlete, Dell lays out all the ways run/walk can improve your training and how to make the most of the method.

If you’re a first-time runner or someone following a couch-to-5K training plan, your run/walk intervals might look like 30 seconds of running followed by a 60-second walk interval.

If you’re a first-time marathoner or a more advanced runner, however, you might run for four minutes followed by 30-second walks. More advanced runners or those going for long distances might also use run/walk intervals during workouts such as Yasso 800s. To do it, run 800 meters at the prescribed pace, but instead of jogging between efforts, walk briskly to recover. This walk interval should be double the amount of time of the hard effort, Dell says.

While run/walk intervals can serve as a speed workout hack to help you get faster and pace more evenly (more on that below), they can improve your running in other ways, too. For example, try 90-second run intervals and 30-second walks for extra recovery on an easy run the day after a long run. This reduces the overall stress of the effort, but still gets your legs turning over so you can move through any soreness without stiffening up, Dell explains.

You can also use run/walk intervals during your weekend long runs to help you conquer the distance.

If you want to run farther distances, “run/walk keeps your heart rate low for long enough that you can maintain pace for a lot longer than you would expect,” says Dell. This makes it a lot more manageable to tackle a half or full marathon for the first time (or if you’re racing the distance again after a long time away).

Dell tells runners that if they can run six continuous miles, they’re capable of completing nine miles using run/walk intervals because the walk breaks reduce the overall intensity and effort of the run. This can provide a smoother transition to the half marathon for runners who just worked up to training for a 5K or 10K.

Run/walk intervals can also help runners increase their long-run distance during half or full marathon training, Dell says. “I’ve had athletes who either could not get over the half marathon distance to save their lives or blew up on runs multiple weeks in a row,” she says, but run/walk helped fix that.

If you tend to “bonk” around mile 13 of a 15-mile long run, using run/walk intervals for the first five miles will help keep your heart rate down longer so you can maintain your pace and build patience with the run. Then, you’ll be in a better position to complete all 15 miles without hitting the wall, Dell explains.

Runners who are just beginning to incorporate interval workouts into their training might struggle to switch between hard and easy paces. “Some people don’t know how to run at different paces. They only know their one pace and that’s kind of it,” says Dell. “So when they get into speedwork, their heart rates just spike so quickly because they’re not used to those faster paces yet.”

If you’re used to training at more intense speeds, but you struggle to stay in zone 2 on easy runs, run/walk can help you keep your pace and your heart rate down. Maintaining 30-second walk breaks and the run interval that works best for you (anywhere from 60 seconds to six minutes, depending on your fitness level and speed) will help keep your heart rate in the right easy zone.

Run/walk intervals can also help speed up recovery, Dell adds. When you’re doing speedwork, you can reduce your injury risk and recover faster by walking—instead of jogging—between efforts.

A lot of the time, runners tend to unknowingly speed up during the jog intervals, which leads to not fully recovering between each effort. That makes them more likely to experience cumulative fatigue, she explains. “This is really important for people who are doing half or full marathons for the first time, because they are just constantly building mileage,” and more work requires more recovery, she says.

Better quality recovery intervals mean better quality speed intervals, too. And walking instead of jogging in between your faster efforts allows you to push harder, both mentally and physically, Dell explains.

“Mentally, you’ll have an easier time pushing hard if you know there’s a true walk break coming. You’ll also have more leg turnover, feel speedier, and get your heart rate down [during the working sets],” Dell says.

Run/walk is also a great tool for splitting up an otherwise monotonous maintenance run, Dell explains. “Maybe it’s a Monday, or it’s cold outside, and you just don’t want to go for your run,” she says. Run/walk intervals not only help you keep your easy pace truly easy, but they also remove the mental pressure of trying to maintain one pace for the entire run.

“It’s mindless: You follow your watch’s beeps [for when to walk and run] and you can just listen to your music. Then all of a sudden, you’ve got your four miles done while leaving your analytical brain out of it,” Dell adds.

Every runner needs to learn how to switch gears between running and brisk walking on marathon race day, whether that’s to grab gels or water, navigate crowded courses, or keep moving if you hit the wall in the later miles, Dell says. “If you’re running the New York City Marathon and all of a sudden you blow up at mile 18 going up some of the bridges, it’s a good idea to learn how to [slow down] and restart your body at any point,” she explains.

Beginner marathoners and seasoned athletes alike can only benefit from adding run/walk to their training schedule. And who knows? You might like it so much, you run/walk an entire race and PR.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8769. What to Do About These High Interest Rates

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this new development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the important part, which is,

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

For most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and new construction alike.

It also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started new companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing new things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

So eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

And that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their plans to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build new factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

All of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

The reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no big deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

The stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

But since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

But remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting new highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:

For most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

This is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

The first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

On the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

Thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build new houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

Remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

But a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

You can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:

What the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:

If you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds currently believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

And if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

With the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

So to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more important are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller issues of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

In the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

Mr. Money Mustache September 5, 2023, 2:56 pm

I’m usually in favor of at least 20%, because when you work out the effective interest rate increase that PMI is hitting you with, it usually works out to a very good return on that extra 10%.

For example, imagine a 500k house, and you are debating between a 50k or 100k downpayment (10 or 20%). And let’s say the interest rate is down at 5%.

If the PMI premium is a typical 0.8% of the loan value $450k, you’d be paying an extra $3600 per year in PMI premiums. Just for the privilege of not putting down the extra $50k.

That’s 7% of the potential extra downpayment that gets eaten up every year!

Or to put it another way, if you put in the second $50k, you are earning 5% in foregone loan interest PLUS 7% in saved PMI premiums. 12% in total, which is the best return around.

It’s a similar return when deciding between a 15 vs 30 year mortgage (the 15 year mortgage provides the extra risk free return). The return decreases the longer one keeps the mortgage, but for most people who move / re-finance within 7 years or so, it’s well worth it.

My brother got a mortgage from Navy Federal Credit Union with no PMI. So those deals are out there. This is not a VA loan, just standard mortgage. I’m thinking other credit unions might offer the same.

A good option at the moment for military people looking to purchase homes is a VA assumption loan. Essentially you “assume” the VA loan of another person instead of getting a new loan at today’s rates. The downside is that the purchase takes much longer, and since interest rates have been going down for decades, it hasn’t made sense to do an assumption loan for decades, so most people aren’t familiar with the process. We’re about 3 months into the process, and it’s looking like end-to-end it is going to take 5-6 months, but we’re assuming a 2.25% interest rate instead of today’s ~7%. You also can’t choose how much your down payment is. You have to have enough cash on hand to pay off whatever the difference is between the purchase price and what the seller has left on the mortgage.

My mortgage is 2.5% – P&I is $886/mo. Last year, we had about 28 years left and the interest was slightly higher than the principal payment each month – about $450/mo. or so in interest. Did a lump sum payment and cut off about 15 years of payments – now almost all my payment goes to the principal. The interest each month is now only about $230/mo.

In this sense, the savings in interest each month is about equal to what I’d be earning if I’d kept the lump sum in a money market. I’ve also got peace of mind because A. if I didn’t make another extra payment, I’ll still have a paid-for house in about 13 years, and B. since the money is already spent on the mortgage, it removes the temptation to find something else to use it on.

So the short answer to your comment is: yes, the front-loaded nature of the mortgage does factor into the equation. From an interest savings perspective, it’s definitely more profitable to pay the mortgage down during the first half of the amortization versus the last half.

As I understand it, the front-loaded nature of interest on a mortgage is just a reflection (the mirror image, maybe) of compound interest. So an extra principal payment in year 1 of a 30 year fixed-rate mortgage has a greater impact than one in year 25 because it has longer to compound, not because it gives a greater rate of return.

If you make an extra payment of $100 this year, next year your balance will be lower by $102.85. And in 27 years your balance will be lower by $100*1.0285^27=$213.56.

But if instead you put $100 in your high-yield savings account, next year you will have $105. So you really will approach the payoff amount faster that way (as long as the interest rate you’re earning remains higher).

You understand it correctly! You don’t pay more or less interest as a percentage of your loan by paying it off early or by paying it for 30 years – when you make extra payments early, you simply borrowed the total amount of money for less time. Naturally you pay less aggregate interest if you pay the loan off early, because you borrowed the total sum for less time. If your mortgage is 5%, for example, the total interest you pay as a percentage of what you borrowed will be 5% regardless of whether you pay off the loan in year 1 or year 30. Amortized payments confuse people into thinking that they’re paying more interest in the beginning than the end – no, you’re paying the percentage of whatever is outstanding. The amortization just allows one to have the same payment over the life of the loan, rather than a huge payment now and a itty bitty payment later. So it appears that you are paying more in interest, but it’s just that the interest that is owed is a greater percentage of the payment amount in the beginning because you owe more money.

In any case, you are totally correct that in a static situation paying yourself $100 into a 5% bank account instead of paying $100 extra to a 2.75% mortgage will earn you the delta (5-2.75 =2.25%) real annual return, compounded. Of course there’s no guarantee the savings return remains at 5%, whereas the interest rate on the fixed mortgage is guaranteed to be 2.75%.

I am based in Germany and snagged a historically low interest rate of .87% on my mortgage. The difference is that it is fixed for 10 years so this business of prediction is indeed quite critical to my short and mid term financial planning.

I have had the mindset of paying off the place as rapidly as possible just as a bit of a hedge on the long term uncertainty of life. Hence, I have a bit of a challenge as interest rate predictions would seem to drive my behavior greatly: Option 1 – pay off a super low return mortgage to hedge a long term increasing rate Option 2 – pay off the minimum on my mortgage and invest the remainder because the delta is so massive due to the historic rate I snagged Option 3 – some hybrid of the two

There’s the option of an accelerated pay-off of my mortgage every year so I have until December to decide as I save throughout the year, but it is always interesting times as I do find I need to develop an opinion on the whole mortgage situation.

Option 2 makes the most sense to me. If you want to be conservative you can always invest the additional funds in some type of interest bearing account — in the US that would be something like FDIC insured CDs currently at over 5%, not sure what the German equivalent might be. Then, after 10 years you can use everything saved in the conservative interest bearing accounts and apply it to the mortgage all at once. Yes, the delta is massive, so take advantage of it if you have the discipline to not spend the money elsewhere!

Interest rates are like the weather, easy conversation with anybody but nothing you can really effect. And if it happens to you, it’s usually not tragic. For most people, excessive focus on interest rates can be distracting from more important decisions / choices.

Most people aren’t $250k/yr+ software types. Most people are teachers, government workers, office workers and even factory workers. There are areas of the USA that are frightfully expensive to live in … housing, taxes, transportation and even the need for private education because of failing schools.

For most people the more important decision is where you live and work and not the interest rate on your mortgage. For example, teacher in San Jose CA might make 15%-20% more than a teacher in East Cobb GA. But a home in San Jose will be close to 4x the price of a home in East Cobb. If you aren’t competing with high comp careers, you will have a nicer home earlier in your career and it will cost way less each month. Not everyone wants or can move across the country, but more should consider it. Even lesser distance choices like Sacramento show the difference in lifestyle potential. That $400k home in East Cobb at 8% w/20% down is about $3k/mo (15yr). That SJ $1.4mil home would be over $8k/mo even if the interest rate was half (4%). And the difference in down payment is huge. And taxes and insurance aren’t even discussed here.

Life is easier and way less stressful if housing cost is zero. The path to zero is faster with lower cost housing in lower cost areas. I’ve seen many extended family members move from high cost NYC and NY State. All have better pay, better homes, better schools and way lower cost of living. Life changing for all of them.

For those who live on normal household incomes, where your home is might be way more important than any interest rate.

As far as investments go, if you are not an experienced financial professional or trader, interest rates are irrelevant. You can’t time interest rates or the market. The 80/20 rule (VTSAX/Bonds) rebalanced annually is the safest path for almost everyone. Anything else is really just a guess and sometimes a guess doesn’t work out well.

Housing costs will never be zero, because you still have to maintain the building. Survey every 8 years, new roof every 50 years, repointing every x years, new y every z years…

ChrisD: absolutely true. A bit of a rhetorical flourish on my part. But the carry cost of the physical structure is usually a modest 1% or 2% annually. You are better off with only this expense vs this plus mortgage.

1. A $400k home is easier to acquire, payoff and maintain then a similar home in a HCOL area that costs $1.4 million. Even with a much higher interest rate on the low priced home.

2. Once a home is owned “free and clear”, life is less stressful. More monthly cash to spend or save. Less likely to be tragically impacted by job interruption or negative financial event.

Where you choose to live has much more impact on your financial security than interest rates. Especially if you are a ‘normal’ person vs the huge income technology guy.

Keep in mind that a HCOL area is generally speaking more desirable than a LCOL area, otherwise it wouldn’t be so expensive. If you’re in REITs, beware of anything involving commercial property right now, including bigger multifamily housing. Unlike regular residential loans, these always wind up financed with ARMs with shorter terms, like 5-year or 7-year. With the rising rates, any of these forced to refinance in the current climate are likely to default or be much less profitable if they do survive. Some are forecasting GFC level crashes, this time on the commercial side as opposed to residential (which should be just fine).

Look at the Return on Assets the REIT (or any company) generates. Is this greater than or less than the interest they’ll have to pay to refinance their debts?

If they are earning less on their assets than it costs to finance the assets, expect losses or dividend cuts as they deleverage. E.g. they are borrowing at 6% to hold assets yielding 3%.

Lots of REITs with negative cash flows are in an unsustainable position. It would make sense for them to start shedding assets that no longer earn their cost of capital instead of burning cash while hoping for rates to fall. But when everyone does that…

Another misconception unrelated to your comment that is worth noting is that if the Fed cuts rates that the 10yr and mortgages will come down.  They will come down some but that is related to the option adjusted spread on the mortgage (don’t worry about what that part means, that’s maybe a 0.5%-0.75% swing factor).  Mortgages price off of longer dated treasury rates (~10yr treasury or blend of 5 and 10yr) and these are already baking in a series of cuts beginning in 2024.  So the cuts would need to be more significant than people expect to move mortgage rates significantly.  In other words, if the Fed cuts short term rates in an orderly fashion to 3.5% mortgages might not move all (aside from that option adjusted spread) and the yield curve might just look normal again.

## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead. You've already spent three days eating ramen in Tokyo — a stopover you added to your award ticket for a mere 5,000 extra points. This isn't a once-in-a-lifetime splurge. This is what the ChooseFI community calls a **nearly free** trip, engineered through one of the most underappreciated sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. To put that in FI terms: if you value your points at even the low end of that range — 5.7 cents per point — 75,000 Aeroplan points are worth **$4,275 in travel**. At the high end, you're looking at **$10,725**. That's a portfolio-level return on the credit card spending and transfer partners you've already been accumulating. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. The program is essentially inviting you to stack experiences on a single award, and the ChooseFI community is the group paying close enough attention to accept that invitation.

The core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

Here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. You've essentially purchased two separate international business class flights for the price of one, plus a nominal surcharge.

The other critical piece: Aeroplan charges zero fuel surcharges on partner awards. This was a deliberate policy decision in the 2020 relaunch and it's a massive advantage. Programs like British Airways Avios and Singapore KrisFlyer can add $500–$1,500 in surcharges to long-haul business class awards. With Aeroplan, you pay government taxes only — typically $50–$150 on most itineraries.

You don't need to fly Air Canada or hold an Air Canada credit card to access this. Aeroplan accepts transfers from several major flexible currency programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is your best friend here because transfers are instant, which matters when you're racing to book a specific award seat before someone else claims it. If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, your UR points can become Aeroplan points in seconds.

The booking window is 355 days out, which gives you nearly a full year of planning runway — a significant advantage for families coordinating schedules or travelers targeting peak periods in Tokyo or Singapore. Partner award availability on Aeroplan is generally solid for the Star Alliance network, with business class seats on ANA, Japan Airlines (where applicable), and Singapore Airlines routes opening up regularly. Availability scores a 4 out of 5 for this sweet spot, which reflects genuine accessibility rather than theoretical possibility.

Never transfer points until you have confirmed, bookable award space in hand. Go to aeroplan.com and use the flight search tool. Select "Business" class, enter your origin and destination (e.g., Toronto YYZ to Singapore SIN), and search for one-way awards. Aeroplan's search engine will show you available partner space directly — you don't need a separate search on partner airline websites, though checking ana.co.jp or singaporeair.com for business class availability can help you triangulate what's open before logging into Aeroplan.

Look for awards showing Star Alliance partner carriers (ANA, Singapore Airlines, and others depending on routing). The system will display the points cost and any routing options. Aeroplan's booking window opens 355 days in advance, so set a calendar reminder to search the moment your target travel window becomes available.

Once you've found an outbound flight you like (e.g., Toronto → Tokyo), call Aeroplan at 1-800-361-5373 or use the online multi-city search to add a stopover at your midpoint city. A stopover is any connection exceeding 24 hours. The system will add 5,000 points to your base award cost. Confirm the full itinerary shows both the Tokyo stopover segment and the onward Tokyo → Singapore flight in the cabin class you want.

Note: Online booking for complex multi-city awards with stopovers sometimes requires a phone call to complete. Budget 30–45 minutes for the call and have your routing clearly written out before you dial.

Determine which flexible currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards, transfer to Aeroplan first — it's instant. Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners," select Air Canada Aeroplan, and complete the transfer. Points appear in your Aeroplan account immediately.

If using Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One, or Bilt, initiate the transfer and expect a 1–2 day processing window. Have your Aeroplan member number ready. Do NOT transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1.

Once your points land in your Aeroplan account, return to aeroplan.com and complete the booking within the same browser session if possible. Pay the government taxes and fees with a credit card that earns rewards on travel purchases. Taxes on a routing like YYZ → NRT → SIN are typically in the $100–$200 range — no fuel surcharges.

After booking, download or screenshot your itinerary confirmation. Verify the cabin class on each segment. Check in on the Aeroplan website 24 hours before each flight and confirm your seat assignments. For the stopover city, you are responsible for your own accommodation — budget accordingly, and consider this the best "forced layover" you'll ever take.

A stopover is a deliberate break in your journey at a connecting city, where you stay for more than 24 hours before continuing to your final destination. Most loyalty programs treat stopovers as separate tickets, requiring you to pay miles for each segment independently. Aeroplan breaks this convention by allowing one free stopover on one-way awards, meaning your connecting city becomes a bonus destination at zero additional mileage cost. For example, a flight from New York to Tokyo with a 5-day stopover in Istanbul costs the same 75,000 Aeroplan points as flying directly — but you get to explore Istanbul for nearly a week as part of the trip. The stopover must be at a connection point that makes geographic sense for your routing, but with 26+ Star Alliance airlines and hundreds of hub cities, the options are vast.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's build out a specific redemption so the math becomes undeniable.

The Itinerary: You depart Toronto Pearson (YYZ) on an ANA Boeing 787-9 bound for Tokyo Narita (NRT). You've built in a 3-day stopover in Tokyo — enough time for a morning at Tsukiji, an evening in Shinjuku, and a day trip to Nikko. Then you board a Singapore Airlines flight from NRT to Singapore Changi (SIN) in Business Class.

The Cash Price: A business class itinerary covering this exact routing — YYZ to NRT to SIN — retails in the range of $8,000 to $10,000, depending on season and carrier. Booking two separate one-way tickets (YYZ-NRT and NRT-SIN) in business class would easily exceed that, often landing closer to $10,000–$12,000 combined.

The Points Cost: 70,000 Aeroplan points for the base award + 5,000 for the stopover = 75,000 points total, plus approximately $120–$180 in government taxes. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP Calculation: At a midpoint cash value of $9,000, your 75,000 points are generating 12 cents per point. Even at the conservative $8,000 end, you're at 10.7 cents per point — well within the documented 5.7–14.3 cent range and significantly above the ChooseFI rule of thumb of 2 cents per point for most redemptions.

On the ANA 787-9 YYZ–NRT segment, you're in ANA's Business Staggered seat — a fully flat bed with direct aisle access, Japanese hospitality, and one of the best business class dining experiences in the sky. The Tokyo stopover is yours to explore however you like. Then Singapore Airlines' Business Class on the NRT–SIN leg offers its own benchmark product — a refined seat, excellent service, and arrival into Changi, consistently ranked the world's best airport.

You've visited two of Asia's most celebrated cities, flown on two world-class airlines, slept flat across the Pacific, and your out-of-pocket cash cost was under $200. That is the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in its purest form.

Tokyo in cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and autumn foliage season (November) books up incredibly fast — even in business class. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 355 days before your target departure and search the moment Aeroplan's window opens. Partner award space on popular routes gets claimed quickly.

Because Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Aeroplan instantly, you can hold an award seat without pre-positioning points in your account. Find the space first, then transfer exactly what you need. This is a significant tactical advantage over programs that require 2–5 day transfer windows.

Aeroplan allows open jaw routing. You can fly INTO Tokyo and OUT of Singapore on separate awards, pairing this business class redemption with a separate economy or business award home. Build your Southeast Asia trip so you land in one city and depart from another — no backtracking, better geography, same award pricing framework.

This is the single most common mistake in all of travel rewards. If you transfer 75,000 Chase UR to Aeroplan and then discover the award space disappeared, you cannot transfer back. Chase points are gone. Confirm bookable space first, transfer second, book third.

Marriott transfers to Aeroplan at a 3:1 ratio — meaning you need 225,000 Marriott points to generate 75,000 Aeroplan points. That's an extraordinarily poor ratio for this redemption. Use Chase, Amex, Capital One, or Bilt instead.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining. The Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly. Build your Aeroplan balance through the transfer partners rather than flying Air Canada itself — the flexibility is far more valuable.

Unlike many programs that expire your miles after 12–18 months of inactivity, Aeroplan points never expire. This means you can accumulate slowly and deliberately — a natural fit for the FI community's patient, systematic approach to building travel rewards balances.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers with a genuine interest in Asia — specifically anyone who has ever dreamed of Japan and Southeast Asia in the same trip without paying for two separate premium tickets. If your travel bucket list includes Tokyo and Singapore in the same itinerary, this is the single most efficient way to get there in business class.

Minimum points needed: ~75,000 Aeroplan points (70,000 base + 5,000 stopover). Build this through Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, or Bilt transfers.

For the FI-minded traveler, this is a high-ROI, low-cash-cost adventure that fits perfectly into a strategy of saving aggressively while experiencing the world nearly free.

## Why This Is Rated Moderate — And How to Handle It This sweet spot earns a **moderate difficulty** rating — not because the math is complicated, but because the booking process has more moving parts than a simple domestic award. **What makes it moderate:** 1. **Complex routing with a stopover** — Aeroplan's online tool doesn't always handle multi-city stopover bookings cleanly. You may need to call Aeroplan to finalize the itinerary, which adds a step and requires you to have your routing clearly planned before you dial. 2. **Partner award availability** — You're booking seats on ANA, Singapore Airlines, or other Star Alliance carriers, not Air Canada. Partner space is real and accessible (this scores a 4/5 for availability), but it requires searching specifically for it on aeroplan.com and sometimes triangulating with partner airline websites. 3. **Points transfer timing** — You need points in your Aeroplan account before completing the booking, which means coordinating a transfer after confirming space exists. Chase's instant transfer largely solves this problem. **Three tips to make it manageable:** - **Use aeroplan.com's multi-city search first** to understand what routing options exist before calling. Come to any phone call with a primary and backup itinerary already researched. - **Book 6–12 months out** using the 355-day window. More availability, more flexibility, less stress. - **Do one transfer before you need to** — move a small amount of points to Aeroplan just to practice the process and verify your accounts are linked. If you've successfully booked a domestic business class award before, this is a natural next step. The complexity is manageable, and the reward — business class across two ocean crossings with a Tokyo stopover — is absolutely worth the extra 45 minutes of work.

Identify your final destination and choose a stopover city that lies along a logical routing. Popular stopover cities include Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), Tokyo (ANA hub), Frankfurt (Lufthansa hub), and Zurich (Swiss hub). The stopover city must be a connection point that Aeroplan considers valid for your route.

On aircanada.com, use the multi-city search option. Enter your origin to the stopover city as the first segment, and the stopover city to your final destination as the second segment. Set business class and search. The system will show you combined availability and pricing with the stopover included.

Once you confirm availability, transfer the required points from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant to 24 hours), Amex Membership Rewards (1-3 days), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming both segments have availability.

Follow the booking flow on aircanada.com, selecting both segments. The system will recognize the stopover and price it as a single one-way award. Confirm the total mileage cost matches the one-way rate for your destination — the stopover should add zero additional miles.

With up to 45 days at your stopover city, plan accommodations and activities. Consider using hotel points for your stopover stay — Hyatt points in Istanbul or IHG points in Singapore pair well with an Aeroplan stopover. The stopover is the bonus trip, so treat it as a mini-vacation within your larger journey.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on one-way awards. This is more than enough time for a genuine visit to your stopover city. You can stay as briefly as 24 hours (anything less is considered a connection, not a stopover) or as long as 45 days before continuing to your final destination.

No. The free stopover on a one-way award is included at no additional mileage cost. Your total point cost is determined by the origin-to-final-destination pricing, not by the number of stops along the way. A flight from New York to Bangkok with a stopover in Istanbul costs the same as New York to Bangkok direct.

Aeroplan prices round trips as two one-way tickets. Each one-way award allows one free stopover, so a round-trip booking can include up to two stopovers — one on the outbound and one on the return. This effectively turns a round trip into a four-destination itinerary.

Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian, and THAI Airways impose significant fuel surcharges on award tickets that can add $100 to $400 per segment. To minimize out-of-pocket costs, route through carriers with no or low surcharges: Turkish Airlines, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines (on most routes), and United. Check the fare breakdown before confirming your booking.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Aeroplan's free stopover on one-way awards is a genuinely unique feature that no other major North American loyalty program offers. The ability to spend a week in Istanbul, Singapore, or Tokyo as a free add-on to your business class award makes Aeroplan one of the most valuable programs in the travel rewards ecosystem. Combine this with access to 26+ Star Alliance carriers, online booking for stopover routings, and 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, and Bilt, and you have a program that delivers outsized value for the ChooseFI community. Build a transferable points balance, identify your dream two-destination trip, and let Aeroplan's stopover rule turn one award into two vacations.

#8767. The GLP Coaching Institute Certification: Frequently Asked Questions

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a comprehensive professional education program developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute in partnership with Precision Nutrition. It combines GLP-1 science with evidence-based behaviour-change methods and practical coaching skills to help health, fitness, nutrition, and medical professionals better support clients using GLP-1 medications.

GLP-1 medications are changing the way clients eat, exercise, and recover. And many professionals are facing questions their existing education hasn’t fully prepared them to answer.

This certification helps close that gap, with specialized training in GLP-1 physiology, nutrition, exercise, recovery, and coaching. From navigating reduced appetite and protecting strength to supporting long-term maintenance, you’ll use the Five GLP Types to decide where to start and learn how to adapt your approach to the person in front of you.

For example, a client with a dramatically reduced appetite may struggle to get enough protein and essential nutrients. Someone who’s losing weight quickly may also be losing strength or struggling to recover from workouts that used to feel manageable.

Others may experience medication-related side effects, changes in their relationship with food, or plateaus that require a different approach.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

It also means recognizing when a client’s needs go beyond coaching and require input from their prescriber or another healthcare professional.

#8766. Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family)

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:

1. Procrastination is Expensive — Swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes

27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

29. There Are Steps — Once you have finished your first sprint triathlon, take the following actions (in order): a) Sign up for an Ironman, b) Sign up for a Hyrox, c) Advertise your coaching services.

30. Triathlon = Procrastination (Always) — Finally, swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.
