#8764. REI vs. Dick’s Sporting Goods Black Friday Deals, Which Is Better?

The two brands are known for wilding out on sales, but here’s how to find the best deals.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Your cart has been sitting there since October, and I get it. I’ve got a few (hundred) tabs open myself. As someone with many marathons, a few ultras, and more halfs and 5Ks than I can count, I can tell you the real Black Friday question isn’t whether to buy shoes and running gear; it’s where. REI and Dick’s are two of the names that come up the most often, and they handle the holiday very differently. REI is again giving its employees a paid day off on Friday, November 27, so its deals land early. Dick’s has typically stretched its sale across the weekend. Deciding who has the best deals comes down to these two questions: What are you actually shopping for, and how much do you need? Here’s how the deals stack up.

One thing both brands are doing, and doing pretty well, is taking some big-name running shoes and discounting them hard. Think Hoka, Asics, and Brooks top trainers with discounts of $50 or more, with deeper discounts on previous years’ models. The deals don’t match model to model, and each outlet has different shoes at different prices. For example, REI offers steeper discounts on Hoka, and Dick’s has better pricing on brands like Adidas.

The Hoka Bondi 9 is a favorite among distance runners, especially those with flatter feet. It has a supercritical foam midsole that makes it light and responsive, with a snug fit, a generously padded collar, and comfortable, max-stack cushioning. It’s a big improvement over the Bondis of antiquity, and it’s one of their most popular shoes overall. And the price difference between REI and Dick’s is significant, with REI the clear winner.

Can’t go wrong with the ultra-comfortable Adizero Evo SL from Adidas. It’s fun to run in; it’s bouncy, responsive, and keeps you happy on long runs. Dubbed by Jeff Dengate as the Shoe of the Year for 2025, this trainer remains one of our most beloved shoes of the past few years.

The On Cloudmonster 3 is the perfect mix of firm and cushioned, keeping you supported on your longest efforts, whether walking or running. It’s a max-cushioned trainer with On’s CloudTec technology that compresses and rebounds with every strike, making it responsive, a bit bouncy, and ready for high mileage.

REI is also known for its Co-op line of gear. It’s their own, high-quality gear that comes in at terrific prices. For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, many of those items are discounted even further, making it hard to say no to already affordable goodies. REI also offers a variety of smaller brands like Rabbit, which they are able to offer on sale. If you’re into smaller brands, or you’re a big fan of Co-op, REI is the place to hit up.

Rabbit makes great UPF-rated long sleeves that are perfect for layering on cooler days or staying cool in the sun on hotter days. This one has one of my favorite features—a watch panel that lets you wear the shirt over your hands with thumb holes, so you can still see your watch. The fabric is buttery, the seams are sealed, so they’re not itchy or irritating, and they launder like a dream.

REI makes really good hydration vests, often in a more expansive size range than other brands. I’ve tested this one, and I like it a lot. It has space for a bladder and two flasks, plus room for snacks, gear, and whatever you happen to take off during your run because you’ve overheated.

Some of the biggest sales at Dick’s Sporting Goods are on its biggest-ticket items like treadmills, running watches, and other exercise equipment. These are categories that REI doesn’t touch as much, and some not at all (treadmills). This area is where Dick’s really shines. You could get hundreds off this time of year, and you should take full advantage.

This is truly one of my favorite “get-up-and-run” treadmills, and for 40 percent off, it’s tripping into “cheap” treadmill territory. It’s a solid treadmill with a good-size deck, plenty of connectivity, incline, and speed, all at a fabulous price tag.

Suunto has improved so much over the past few years, and this is one of the best examples. It’s a dynamic, multisport running watch with terrific GPS, battery life, connectivity, and a family of apps to help keep you connected. It’s also one of the better-looking running watches available, and while that might not be the most important thing, it’s still worth considering.

Both brands have fantastic Black Friday discounts, but they look pretty different. Dick’s has the upper hand on big-ticket items, but their shoes are a bit more expensive. REI wins on shoe price, and in the smaller labels and private-label brands they’re known for. And both stores carry shoe brands the other doesn't. In the end, it’s about picking your faves and knowing what you’re shopping for.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#8763. Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family)

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

And we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

First, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Once you know your purpose, Hopkins says, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins says, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

You don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

So, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

Another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

If you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

From there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

#8762. Running for Time vs. Distance: Experts Explain Which Is Better for Your Goals

The pros and cons of training by minutes versus miles.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether your goal is to run a marathon or simply improve your fitness, following a solid training plan will help you stay consistent as you work toward that goal. But with so many options to choose from, finding the right training plan can feel tricky.

So where do you start? Consider this: Most plans fall into the very broad categories of time-based versus distance-based running. In other words, a plan prescribes runs in terms of minutes or in terms of miles. There’s no clear evidence that one is inherently superior for race-day performance, but each approach does have specific advantages and disadvantages.

To help you determine whether time-based running or distance-based running is right for you, we tapped three experts to explain the pros and cons of each. They break down exactly what to consider so you can pick the type of training plan that best fits your schedule, preferences, ability level, and race goals.

Distance-based plans, or those that provide specific mileage goals for each workout, are incredibly common. That’s in part because they make a lot of sense for runners training to race a certain distance, such as a 5K, 10K, half marathon, or full marathon. Runners need to prepare their bodies for the specific mileage of their chosen race, Janet Hamilton, CSCS, an exercise physiologist and the founder and head coach of Running Strong, tells Runner’s World. And following a distance-based plan is a great way to ensure you’re getting in the right number of miles.

Aside from preparing you physically for a race, distance-based plans can provide a powerful mental boost. Knowing you’ve successfully run a given distance before you toe the starting line—whether that’s logging three miles prior to attempting a 5K, or 20 miles in advance of a marathon—can give you confidence that you’ll be able to finish the race you’re gearing up for, says Jacob Phillips, a Texas-based run coach with RunDoyen.

Distance-based plans can also clue you into your current performance levels. For example, if you run six miles at a hard effort, you’ll get a good grasp on your 10K abilities. “You know exactly where you stand over the prescribed distance,” explains Ken Rideout, a masters marathon world champion and nationally best-selling author of the memoir, Everything You Want Is on the Other Side of Hard.

The biggest downside of a distance-based plan: If it’s not coupled with instructions on how to pace yourself or what effort level to strive for, then it’s up to you to manage those details. And in Hamilton’s experience, many runners, when left to their own devices, complete their workouts at lactate threshold pace. That’s about the same effort at which you’d race a 10K or half marathon—much faster than you want to do your daily runs.

While there are certainly benefits to running at faster paces, you don’t want to miss out on all the perks of easy-pace running. Keeping your daily runs at a comfortable, conversational effort helps develop slow-twitch muscle fibers, improves running economy, and may even reduce your injury risk.

Many beginner-friendly plans and run/walk programs use time as the main training parameter. One perk of this approach is that timed runs can be “a lot less intimidating” than distance workouts, says Rideout. “When you’re running a prescribed distance, you can’t help but notice, what was my pace? What were my mile splits?” he explains. But the format of a time-based run automatically reduces the prominence of those metrics, which can be helpful if you’re just easing into a running routine.

Experienced runners might find similar benefits to this approach. For folks who get frazzled by having to check their mileage throughout a run, or those who get obsessive about pace, a time-based plan may be a soothing alternative. “It’s not as stressful,” Phillips explains. “I think there’s a simplicity to saying, ‘Hey, you’re going to go out and just run for half an hour,’” without having to worry about completing a certain route or number of miles.

A time-centric approach can also encourage athletes to embrace easy-effort runs because it removes intrinsic pressure to run hard, says Phillips. After all, if time is the only goal, it doesn’t matter how fast you go—you’ll be successful in that day’s workout by simply moving for the prescribed duration.

This can also make time-based training a good idea for busy runners. Say you only have 30 minutes today to break a sweat. With a duration-focused plan, you’ll be able to complete your planned workout, even if variables such as the terrain you’re running over or your energy levels that day impact your usual pace. No matter what happens, you’re done in 30 minutes.

Opting for timed runs can also make sense for folks who are trail running in off-the-grid locations where there are no mile markers and GPS devices don’t always function well, says Hamilton. Instead of fixating on how far they’ve run—which may be challenging if not impossible given the circumstances—runners can be successful by simply going out for a certain number of minutes.

A duration approach may come in handy for traveling runners, too, says Hamilton. When you’re in an unfamiliar location, there’s no need to expend effort trying to figure out how to make a five-mile loop from your hotel. Instead, you can run out-and-back for 45 minutes and call it a day.

Lastly, because there’s less emphasis with time-based runs on achieving a certain pace, they can help you “get into different heart-rate zones and stay in a specific zone for a prescribed period of time,” says Rideout. This can be beneficial in improving your overall fitness, he explains.

Time-centric running isn’t for everyone. As we mentioned, if you’re training for a particular distance, a plan focused solely on duration may not give you the race-specific preparation—or confidence—you need to achieve your goal.

Additionally, time-based plans might not be the best fit for runners who are strongly motivated by tracking their daily and weekly mileage or hitting new distance-based milestones.

When comparing time versus distance running, know that “both ways can be very, very beneficial,” says Phillips. It all just boils down to finding the right plan that fits your goals and lifestyle.

In general, new runners will likely find success with a time-based approach, while more experienced runners, especially those targeting a specific goal time in a race, “tend to do a little bit better with a volume-based approach,” says Phillips.

Your personality and preferences for a training plan may also influence which philosophy to follow. “As a coach, I like saying ‘We did X amount of miles this week, and next week we’re going to do X amount of miles,’” says Phillips, noting that many of the runners he coaches also prefer to track their progress via distance logged week to week.

On the flip side, “there are some people who just don’t want that,” says Phillips. “They don’t want the stress of comparing week to week or even day to day, so I think it just comes down to what you enjoy more.”

Hamilton, for her part, tends to recommend plans that combine time and distance prescriptions—for example, run six miles in 60 minutes—because she finds this hybrid approach helps her athletes develop confidence in running certain distances while also keeping their pace in check.

Rideout is of the mindset that a well-rounded training plan will include both types of runs. “I try to always keep things fresh, keep my body guessing, and try to optimize performance all the time,” he explains. Regularly introducing different types of training—via time-centric workouts and distance-focused runs—is a good way to ensure your body continues to adapt and improve.

No matter what plan you choose, you can always sub one time-focused run for a distance-based workout, and vice versa, if you think it helps your mindset that day.

Jenny is a Boulder, Colorado-based health and fitness journalist. She’s been freelancing for Runner’s World since 2015 and especially loves to write human interest profiles, in-depth service pieces and stories that explore the intersection of exercise and mental health. Her work has also been published by SELF, Men’s Journal, and Condé Nast Traveler, among other outlets. When she’s not running or writing, Jenny enjoys coaching youth swimming, rereading Harry Potter, and buying too many houseplants.

Your guide to smarter recovery—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

What you do to recover between runs matters just as much as the miles themselves. But knowing what your body needs isn’t always straightforward. Should you head out for an easy run or take the day off? Is that soreness normal, or a sign of an injury about to derail everything? And which recovery tools are actually worth the hype?

This guide helps you navigate those decisions, starting with the fundamentals. Plus, we’ll help you choose a training plan to ease back into running after a race, your offseason, or an injury (both minor and burdensome).

Recovery doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require giving the basics as much attention as your workouts. #8760. She Trained Through Alaskan Winters to Run a Sub-3 Marathon. These Strategies Helped Her Fight the Cold and Stay Consistent.

Snow, ice, and short days didn’t stop Michelle Baxter from regular runs outdoors.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When winter arrives, it’s tempting to put your running goals on hold until the temperatures warm up, the days get longer, and the roads clear. Cold temperatures make it harder to leave a warm bed, while snow and ice can turn a familiar route into a much slower—and more slippery—run.

For months at a time, Michelle Baxter’s running routes in Anchorage, Alaska, were covered in packed snow and ice. After a snowstorm, plows could take days to reach every neighborhood, and by then, cars had compressed the fallen snow onto the roads. Even after the plows came through, the slick surface often remained.

Baxter—now an RRCA- and V.02-certified run coach—spent 15 years living in Alaska and training through winters like these, figuring out how to keep running through harsh, unmotivating conditions.

She trained for 12 marathons in that time, continuing to build fitness year after year. Eventually, she even achieved her most ambitious running goal: breaking three hours in the marathon. After eight years of attempting to break the barrier—and a heartbreakingly close 3:01:14 at Humpy’s Marathon in Anchorage in August 2021—Baxter finally ran a 2:58:24 at the California International Marathon in December 2021. She has since lowered her PR to 2:56:57 at the Indianapolis Monumental Marathon.

Your winter running routes may not be covered in snow and ice for six months straight, but chances are you’ll face your own challenges as the temperature drops in the coming weeks and months. The good news: Baxter’s experience can help you navigate tough terrain and make the most of your training.

Here’s how you can put her lessons to work this winter so when the ice thaws, you’re ready to run your fastest race yet.

What you wear can make or break a winter run, Baxter says. When you’re too cold, too warm, or worried about taking a spill around every tight corner, it’s hard to focus on any other aspect of the run. Baxter spent years figuring out what works, and her gear advice starts with two essentials: finding reliable footwear and appropriate layers for the conditions.

In Anchorage, finding reliable footing was Baxter’s biggest winter challenge. She initially resisted buying studded shoes, assuming they wouldn’t make much difference. But once she tried them, she was surprised by how much more confident she felt in every step.

For packed snow, Baxter often wore regular trainers fitted with screws in the outsoles, which she added herself.

On sheer ice, Baxter preferred shoes made with built-in carbide studs; she swears by the Icebug brand. “You can wear these shoes and make a 90-degree turn and feel so confident running on ice—like sheer ice,” Baxter says. “They were a game-changer for me.”

You may not encounter sheets of ice on your regular running routes, but consider the conditions you encounter most often and look for an option suited to them.

Now living in Minnesota, Baxter says she reaches for studded shoes if she expects at least half of a run to cover potentially snowy or icy ground. She notes that while the shoes may be slightly less comfortable than your normal trainers, protecting your body from harm is the number-one priority during the winter months of training.

“I just think it’s worth it to feel confident running on the slippery surfaces and not risk injuring yourself,” she says.

One of the most common winter gear mistakes Baxter sees runners make is overdressing. It’s easy to look out the window, see cold weather, and pull on every layer you own in an effort to stay warm on the run. But remember you’ll warm up once you start moving.

Baxter’s rule of thumb echoes the advice of other run coaches: Start your run feeling a little chilly. After about 10 minutes, you should warm up and feel comfortable for the rest of the run.

Don’t forget to consider the wind, too; Baxter generally recommends dressing for the wind chill temperature. She recalls learning this lesson during one particularly windy Alaska run when she dressed for the ambient temperature rather than the wind chill temperature and ended up feeling sick from potential hypothermia.

If you’re unsure where to start when it comes to gearing up for a winter run, use our temperature-based layering guide, then pay attention to how you feel after each run. Were you still cold after warming up? Did you get sweaty and uncomfortable? Use your responses to adjust your layers on your next run.

For Baxter, keeping her legs warm as temperatures approached subzero was a recurring problem. She first turned to wearing multiple pairs of tights, which helped with the cold, but the layers restricted her movement. Eventually, she found a thick, fleece-lined pair of running tights that solved the problem, recommending them to other runners for temperatures ranging from 15 all the way down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit.

She made a similar change on top: Instead of wearing a base layer, fleece layer, and wind layer, she found a high-quality warm jacket to wear over a base layer.

Your biggest frustration might be cold hands or wet feet. For these issues, Baxter suggests putting hand warmers in your gloves, running-specific wool socks, and a waterproof shoe.

For visibility during the winter months, Baxter wears a lighted vest. She began treating it as a non-negotiable in her running wardrobe after noticing, as a driver, how much easier it was to see runners wearing blinking lights rather than simple reflective clothing items.

“Investing in a few quality pieces [of winter gear], I think you’re just going to enjoy your run more,” Baxter says. “You’re going to be safer and more comfortable.”

Even with the right layers, leaving your warm house and getting out the door often proves difficult when it’s cold and dark.

Baxter understands the struggle better than most. Anchorage gets less than six hours of daylight during the darkest winter months, and the city’s winter high temps hover around 25 degrees Fahrenheit.

So, how did she keep getting out there? “Running just became a habit of mine,” she says. “It’s how I start my day. I get up, I go for a run.” Even during peak winter in Alaska, Baxter often ran seven days a week simply because it was a part of her daily routine.

Baxter says each individual needs to find what helps them keep going, whether that’s a future goal, a training partner to run alongside, or a plan that lets you check off workouts.

For Baxter, her motivation and discipline to make running a habit often came from looking ahead.

“I just know how important those base miles are during the winter,” she says. “So I know I need to keep putting in the work, keep doing some workouts, because it’s only going to pay off down the road.”

If you have a spring marathon, a summer 10K, or another goal in mind, remind yourself how your winter routine fits into that bigger picture. You can also adjust your expectations for the season: Baxter says it’s okay to scale back during winter if that’s what works for you. A simple maintenance routine can help you arrive at your next training cycle ready to build.

The point is, doing something is better than doing nothing.

A goal months away isn’t always enough to get you out the door on a cold morning. Baxter suggests finding something closer to look forward to, too.

Consider signing up for a winter race, even if it isn’t one of your main events for the year. A Turkey Trot, holiday run, or another low-pressure race with friends can provide a checkpoint and make winter training more fun.

Soon after moving to Anchorage, Baxter joined a training group that held workouts at The Dome, an indoor athletic facility featuring an indoor track. The group helped her settle into the running community while giving her a reason to show up for a workout each week.

Once she developed those friendships, other runners expected her to show up, and those weekly track workouts were no longer optional.

If you’re looking for a similar boost, check for a local run club or training group. A standing workout appointment can give your week structure, while supportive company can make a difficult session feel less daunting.

Baxter generally followed the workouts on her schedule, but she changed where she ran to make them possible. The day after a substantial snowfall, she would head to the treadmill rather than plodding through fresh snow, for example. She also took many of her harder workouts to the treadmill or indoor track, where she felt more comfortable running fast.

Her easy and long runs, meanwhile, almost always happened outside.

You can take the same approach by considering the purpose of the day’s run. If you have a faster workout planned and the outdoors only offers slippery conditions, an indoor option may help you complete it with more confidence. If you’re running easy outside, give yourself room to slow down when conditions make your usual pace unrealistic.

Most of all, remember that one winter is part of a much longer running journey. Baxter’s progress—and eventual sub-three breakthrough—came from conquering multiple training cycles and years of running. The work you do this winter can be another step in that process.

“You simply can’t deny the power of consistently stacking marathon block upon marathon block or just years and years and years of running,” Baxter says. “Endurance running is a long game.”

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#8759. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis)

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

“I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

“If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”

#8758. Nike Shoes Aren’t Just for the Elites. These Are the 10 Best Trainers Our Team Tested.

The Swoosh is known for innovation (Vaporfly 4%, anyone?). Here’s our list of the best Nike shoes on sale now.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 11, 2026: The long-awaited Alphafly 4 is out now—and selling out fast. You can find more options at sites like Fleet Feet.

Brownie points if you knew the waffle iron and Swoosh go a long way back. It was the early 1960s when University of Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports (BRS) with one of his runners, Phil Knight. BRS was a proprietor of Onitsuka Tiger’s athletic shoes before manufacturing its own product. Depending on who you believe, Bowerman customized running shoes using a waffle iron either in the early 1960s, when he gave pairs to his athletes to compete in, or in 1971, the same year BRS was renamed Nike, after the Greek goddess of victory. And that’s how legends are born (and shoe awards are given).

You can read Knight’s side of the story by reading Shoe Dog, or watch Prefontaine or Without Limits for a more dramatic tale about one of the University of Oregon’s star athletes with Nike’s origin story in the background (the 1997 movie is the superior of the two, IMHO). Since the dawn of the Swoosh, the brand has rocked the running industry boat with its innovations. In the past 10 years, for instance, the Vaporfly 4% appeared on the scene, creating mass ripples of new World Athletics guidelines, academic studies on super shoes and running economy, and world records such as the late Kelvin Kiptum’s superhuman 2:00:35 at the 2023 Chicago Marathon.

Back in my early days at Runner’s World in 2018, the first Nike shoe I tested—and ran in—was the inimitable Vaporfly. The shoe left an impression, causing me to never turn back from racing marathons in carbon-fiber-plated trainers. But one thing that made me move on to other brands’ super shoe iterations was the narrow fit and unstable ride of Nike’s racers. All the more to show the brand’s ever-continuing evolution into being the best as well as more inclusive.

Battle of the Brands: The Best Brooks Running Shoes ● The Best Adidas Running Shoes ● The Best Mizuno Running Shoes

I’ve run and raced in several of the shoes on this list. As a Nike newb when I was hired at RW, I was schooled in the Swoosh’s indelible influence on the running industry—our magazine’s first issue came out six years after Nike’s renaming—and witnessed the dawn of the super shoe. All of the shoes on this list were tested by members of our 300-and-counting test team of local runners. They come from all walks of life, varying by gait pattern, arch height, and footstrike.

The Vomero 18 is the first Nike shoe I ran in that didn’t initially feel like a Nike trainer. The shoes fit wide. Its midfoot is broader than the narrow lasts I associate with the Swoosh. Running in the Vomero 18 for the first time, I noticed two things: this shoe is über-soft and doesn’t cause my ankles to turn inward.

This Vomero is the starting point of the brand’s other cushioned shoes, which also include this list’s Vomero Plus and soon-to-be-released Vomero Premium. The story behind this new fit is that Nike shoe development listened to women, applying their fit preferences to both the women’s and men’s versions. Turns out men like the new last too, according to a Nike rep I spoke with recently on the phone.

The Vomero 18 serves as a long-run trainer, daily trainer, and recovery shoe. The cushioning reminds me of Brooks’s Glycerin Max; it’s marshmallowy but responsive. The energy return is still there instead of being zapped like a sponge turning your runs into a slog.

“Hands down these are the best shoes I’ve tested!” said shoe tester Casey Green, a 7:00 pacer who previously tested the Pegasus Plus. “Despite all the extra cushioning the ride was incredibly smooth, responsive, and the shoe never felt weighed down despite the added padding. Every mile I ran in them felt great and slight accelerations or faster average paces were no problem.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Winflo has always been a solid pick for beginners and high school runners. The price is an absolute steal well below the now-standard $170. But the shoe doesn’t feel cheap. Its plush cushioning, which Nike revved up with the twelfth iteration by adding even more Cushlon 3.0 foam underfoot, is fantastic for base building, long runs, or those jobs that require hours of standing.

A small knock is that Nike fit. Unlike the updated Vomero 18 and Structure 26, the Winflo 12 still has that classic Nike foot shape that’s too narrow for some. Sizing up will help alleviate the constriction. It’s worth it for the price and bouncy ride.

Shop Men’s nike.com | Shop Women’s nike.com

The Structure 26 has a few key updates that make it the stability shoe you shouldn’t sleep on. It’s me: I’m the one who slept on it. This is because Nike isn’t at the forefront of my mind when I recommend stability trainers. Lesson learned: the Structure 26 isn’t a shoe to forget. It provides reliable but subtle support for overpronators and neutral runners looking for more guidance, as well as a responsive ride. And it’s relatively cheap for a premium trainer.

The shoe now has ReactX foam, the same foam in the Pegasus 41 and Vomero 18. The foam delivers more rebound compared to the Structure 25’s Cushlon 3.0. An internal midfoot fit band—the triangular structure you can see on either side of the shoe—along with overlays brushed on the sides provide support. The Air Zoom bag was removed in the forefoot and replaced with blown rubber on the outsole to encourage smoother heel-toe transitions. Finally, the upper is cozier too. Nike padded up the collar and tongue for more cushioned touch points and a more secure fit.

Testers liked the shoe for its versatility and used it as their daily trainer for all kinds of workouts. “The shoe is an absolute do-it-all workhorse,” said tester Justin Brown. “I wore it for easy runs, and even progressed up to tempo paces and used it for some strides where I was close to sprinting and I feel like the shoe stood up to all of these really well. At the same time the stability nature of the shoe was honestly nailed, and I felt very secure in the shoe at all times even on wet pavement. The ride was smooth and felt cushioned, but there was enough energy return that I didn’t feel like I couldn’t go faster in it.”

Tester Rich Maier also highlighted the shoe’s support. “I was really impressed by the stability that I felt in both my feet and my legs,” he said. “I usually only experience that level of comfort and support with heavier shoes, but these managed to combine stability with a lighter weight shoe.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Even though the ACG Peg Trail isn’t intended for technical trails—that’s what the ACG Zegama Trail is for—our testers still praised the shoe for its capabilities on the unbeaten path.

“What I liked most about the shoe was its low-profile design that really hugged your foot on all the twists and turns out on the trail,” said tester Jeff Kilian. “Traction was exceptional as well. I feel this shoe is in a league all of its own. I would say the closest thing I can compare this Pegasus to is the Altra Timp, they’re both a lightweight shoe with not much cushioning in the sole.”

The lack of cushioning was a low point for some testers who wanted more support in the forefoot.

Despite the desire for more cushioning, they did appreciate the wider fit in the forefoot and toebox, which helped with stability on the trail.

“The fit has vastly improved,” said shoe tester Jessica Huber. “The width is perfect. There is plenty of space in the toes without feeling bulky.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Nike shoe team wanted to make sure the next Pegasus was snappier and springier than the 41. The team added a full-length Air Zoom unit in the midsole, instead of separate units in previous models. This provides better compression throughout the shoe and improved energy return.

“What I like most is that it feels smooth, with a great rolling ride, but also supportive underfoot,” said tester Molly Sunderlin. “It feels easy to run quickly in, but also like I can do a two-hour long run without getting sore underfoot. I am not sure if this has to do with the shape of the heel which has sort of a ‘roll’ feature. It also wraps my foot so well, almost sock-like with cushion in the right spots. I like putting them on.”

Sunderlin is referring to the slightly curved toe of the shoe, which encourages smooth turnover. The shoe has a slightly modified foot shape to create a more accommodating fit in the midfoot and toe area. Still too tight for you? Not to worry; the Pegasus 42 is also available in extra wide.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

If you miss the Peg Turbo, get a load of the Peg Plus. The second iteration of the shoe is speedier and snappier thanks to an exposed Air unit, which we know signals “fast” in a Nike shoe. The unit functions as a carbon plate; it provides propulsion by compressing during forefoot impact. Its exposure gives it room to breathe; Nike reports this Peg Plus has 18 percent more energy return than the previous version.

Nike wanted to make sure this sensation was consistent with all sizes. The bigger the shoe size, the bigger the Air unit. Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate liked the high rebound, but noted the shoe felt slightly heavy compared to other trainers in the speed category.

“That Air unit pushes back against you quickly, letting you feel snappy with your stride,” wrote Dengate in his review. “Sure, it’s heavy, but in that instance it doesn’t feel slow.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Nike’s mission with the Structure Plus was to change our perception of the stability trainer. Instead of a rigid, firm shoe, the brand wanted to make stability more palatable for all. The Structure Plus is lighter than its cousin, the Structure 26, and is more dynamic; instead of a full ReactX midsole, the Plus is dual-foamed with ReactX on the bottom and soft, energetic ZoomX PEBA foam on the top.

All this is housed in a 42mm stack height, which is 4mm taller than the Structure 26. Such a tall height would cause some to doubt the shoe’s support, but Nike widened the platform and implemented a convex flat sidewall with dense cushioning underneath the arch. The result: support for overpronators and neutral runners who want a little more pep in their stability trainer.

“What I liked most about the Nike Structure Plus was the strong sense of support it delivered on every run,” said tester Julian Caiazzo, an overpronator who averages 7:45 training pace. “The shoe felt stable and dependable without ever coming across as stiff or restrictive. It gave me the confidence to settle into my stride, and even with all that structure, the ride still felt smooth and enjoyable. It struck a great balance between guidance and comfort, which is exactly what I look for in a daily trainer.”

I wore the Structure Plus on a couple of long runs, including my 20-miler during my marathon buildup. Unlike the Vomero Plus, which had my feet roll inward on an 18-miler, the Structure Plus kept my form stable despite the growing fatigue in my weary, long-run legs.

Alternatively, runners who want a more grounded feel—and want to save—can opt for the Structure 26 ($145).

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

This super trainer has next-level softness, from its thick—but breathable—cozy upper to its 43mm (heel) of plush, responsive foam underfoot. Its older sibling, the Vomero 18, has a dual-foam midsole with a top layer of ZoomX and bottom layer of ReactX. With the Vomero Plus, Nike went full PEBA, with the midsole using 100 percent ZoomX.

The shoe is lighter than the Vomero 18 and a smidge shorter (the heel on the Vomero 18 hits 44mm), but I honestly couldn’t detect a major difference in the ride. The Vomero Plus is bouncier, yet if you want to save $25, you could stick with the Vomero 18 (your legs will be none the wiser). But if you want to experience the powers of PEBA and can drop some extra cash, just listen to our testers who gave the Vomero Plus top marks. Our very own editorial assistant Michael McDonough will convince you that of the two Vomeros the Plus is the superior.

“The Nike Vomero Plus is one of, if not my favorite shoe that I’ve tested so far,” said McDonough. “The shoe lives up to the ‘plus’ in its name—I tested the Vomero 18s over the winter, and while I thought those were great as well, the Vomero Plus is an upgrade in several ways. Although they have the exact same amount of cushion, the switch from a mix of ReactX and ZoomX foam to purely ZoomX foam is an absolute game changer. The shoes feel lighter, cushier, and faster—and the fact that the shoe was able to improve all three factors at the same time was pretty remarkable.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

How do you update a shoe that broke the marathon world record back in 2023? The Nike team kept the big changes we loved from the Alphafly 3 and transferred them into the Alphafly 4—with minor tweaks. The scooped, spoon-shaped carbon plate is slightly wider to provide more stability. The thin, almost see-through knit upper, Atomknit 2.0, is similar to the previous version’s with the exception of vertical banding to provide a more secure fit in the midfoot area.

The biggest change is in the forefoot. The Air unit is softer and lighter. In his testing, Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes when you push down. This gives the shoe pop and makes the heel-toe transition smoother as it works with the rocker profile.

Is it quieter than past Alphaflys? According to Dengate... quieter. But comparatively louder than other super shoes he’s tested, and squeaky too. We’ll find out more once tester feedback comes in.

Shop Men’s at fleetfeet.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Nike’s All Conditions Gear (ACG) has been around since 1989. This year, the brand introduced a new era of trail shoes under the ACG name. One of them is the ACG Zegama Trail, a shoe meant for tough all-terrain.

The shoe’s exterior makes it look unquestionably built for technical terrain. The ACG Zegama Trail has a durable cool mesh upper and an ankle cuff that functions as a gaiter, keeping debris out of your shoes. It was a favorite feature for our tester, Chris Fisher, who tested the ACG Zegama Trail last winter.

“Best thing about the Nike Zegama’s was getting into them,” he said. “They’ve got a modified gaiter collar design with a more traditional tongue that allows for easily slipping your feet in. The stretch collar does well at keeping debris out of the shoe which was nice with all the snow I was running in.”

A secure lacing system helps with stability on uneven, twisty trails, as does a broader base. The shoe has a wide forefoot and toebox to allow your toes to splay and lend support.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

To help runners pick and choose the soft ride they’re looking for, Nike has reworked its cushioning into three main categories:

Responsive Cushioning: Pegasus line, providing energy return for all-day wear.

Maximum Cushioning: Vomero line, offering ultimate plush comfort for longer runs.

Supportive Cushioning: Structure line, designed for stability and a supportive ride.

Cushlon: A descendent of Phylon foam, Cushlon is a proprietary EVA foam. It’s lighter than standard EVA midsoles, and provides support and springiness underfoot.

ReactX: Created using an injection process, this foam has more rebound than React foam.

ZoomX: Nike lightest and bounciest foam, it is primarily composed of PEBA.

Working in tandem with midsole foam, Zoom Air units are pouches on the shoe filled with air that help with propulsion. Upon landing, the units compress and absorb impact, then spring back to their original shape.

Should I race in the Alphafly or Vaporfly?

Nike’s premium marathon racing shoe is the Alphafly. It has all the bells and whistles, including PEBA, a Flyplate, and Zoom Air units. This means it’s made to withstand that high-mileage. While the Vaporfly can also be your shoe of choice for marathoning, it’s leaner, Zoom Air unit-free, and is built for racing distances as short as the mile.

During Vomero 18 development, the brand used women’s feedback to create “a better shoe for everyone.” Using these findings, the Nike team applied this to both the women’s and men’s models. According to a Nike rep RW spoke with, turns out men liked the adjustments inferred from women’s feedback too.

#8757. Nike’s Goal With the Structure Plus? Make Stability Less Boring

The brand’s classic stability shoe gets the super trainer treatment with a tall stack height, lighter weight, and PEBA added to the midsole.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

How do you change runners’ conception about stability? Last December at The Running Event in San Antonio, Texas, Nike Expert PLM Ashley Campbell held up the answer: the Structure Plus.

“Stability can be boring,” she admitted. The Structure Plus makes it exciting.

The shoe follows the Vomero Plus, a super trainer version of the Vomero 18. The Structure Plus is the super-ified version of the Structure 26. Where the latter is more accessible for $140, the “plus” iteration is the original amplified in every aspect.

The Structure Plus became my chosen shoe for long runs during my 2026 Boston Marathon training cycle. Here’s how the shoe won me over on a 12-miler, and why you should consider trying a stability super trainer.

While developing the Structure Plus, Campbell said the team set out to make the super trainer “more supportive, smoother, softer, and more palatable.”

Tech-wise, you can see how Nike landed on the first three. The shoe’s platform is wider to provide support. A convex flat shape of sidewall provides stability, the density underneath the arch acting as a stabilizer to help with alignment. A dual layer of foams, like in the Vomero Plus, provides a soft, energizing ride.

In terms of making the shoe more palatable, Campbell wanted the Structure Plus to be all-inclusive. “You don’t have to be an overpronator [to run in the shoe.]”

At 42 mm in the heel and 32 mm in the forefoot, it’d make sense if you expected the shoe to be heavy and unstable. But the Structure Plus challenges these notions.

At 10.9 ounces, men’s 10, the shoe is lighter than the Structure 26, which weighs 11.3 ounces. The maximal cushioning is a layer of PEBA-based ZoomX, a soft foam that delivers high rebound (the foam is also in Nike’s premium marathon shoe, the Alphafly), and TPE-based ReactX, a firmer foam that helps stabilize your ride (the same foam found in the Vomero 18).

Despite the high stack height and max cushioning and stability components, the shoe didn’t weigh me down on my runs, nor did it cause my feet to roll. I didn’t feel like I was forced into alignment. The shoes guide you instead of directing your foot.

It was such a contrast after running in the Vomero Plus the weekend before. During those miles, it got to the point where my friends were getting concerned after I tripped over myself for the umpteenth time. My next long run was smooth, all thanks to the Structure Plus for keeping me stable.

I’m a neutral runner, but as the miles pile on, like they do on long runs, my form gets erratic due to fatigue. It’s those later miles where the Structure Plus saves me from hitting the pavement, or worse, benching myself with injury.

Concerning actual overpronators, our testers were satisfied with the support the shoe provided.

“What I liked most about the Nike Structure Plus was the strong sense of support it delivered on every run,” said tester and overpronator Julian Caiazzo. “The shoe felt stable and dependable without ever coming across as stiff or restrictive. It gave me the confidence to settle into my stride, and even with all that structure, the ride still felt smooth and enjoyable.”

Another overpronator, Katherine Thomas, admitted she usually avoids Nike shoes because of their lack of stability. She was pleasantly surprised with the support of the Structure Plus.

If there’s any reason why you should try the Structure Plus, it isn’t just that it’ll change your preconceived notion of a stability shoe; it’ll also change what you think of Nike trainers.

Like Thomas, I also avoided Nike shoes (unless I had to test them) because of their lack of stability and narrow fit. The Structure Plus doesn’t feel like a Nike shoe; there’s no squeezing on the sides of my midfoot, no pinching by my toes. And yet, I reap that quintessential Nike ride, that layer of ZoomX adding more pop to my strides. Those long runs are anything but boring slogs. I can emphatically say that Nike achieved its goal of making stability—and my runs—more exciting.

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

World of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

Now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt

This is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book

Hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Before searching for availability, confirm your points position. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards and check your combined UR balance across all eligible cards. Remember, points from Chase Ink cards can be pooled with your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred. You'll need at least 25,000 points per night you want to book — a five-night trip requires 125,000 points. If you're close but not there, set a target date 3–4 months out and focus earning in the meantime.

Go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:

For adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

Return to hyatt.com, log into your World of Hyatt account, and complete the award booking for your confirmed dates. At checkout, select points as your payment method. You'll pay only minimal government taxes (typically $10–25/night). Keep your confirmation email — it will specify that the all-inclusive meals, beverages, and activities are included.

Award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

The math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

Let's walk through a real family booking so you can see exactly how the numbers work.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

The CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

The Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card

$95 annual fee | Earn 75,000 bonus points

Side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

$95 annual fee | Earn 100,000 bonus points

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card can be used to offset almost any travel expense.
